story_type: space shuttle released from the back of a 747 for an unpowered glide test, historic film
hook: No engines. Then the 747 let it go.
narration: This space shuttle had no engines, and the jumbo jet carrying it just let it go.
It was Enterprise, NASA's first shuttle orbiter, riding on the back of a Boeing 747 over the California desert in 1977.
It had no air breathing engines, so it would have to land like a glider.
The crew armed the release. Houston called go.
Enterprise dropped away and sank toward the dry lakebed with a chase jet beside it.
Over the radio, the call came back that she was flying good.
outcome: Enterprise glided down to the lakebed, and the tests showed the shuttle had acceptable landing performance.
title: Space shuttle released from a 747
question_comment: Would you have flown a spaceship with no engines off the back of a jumbo jet?

facts.claim: First approach and landing tests, air launched from the back of a 747
facts.source_quote: Dryden Center undertook the first approach and landing tests of the space shuttle, air launching it from the back of a Boeing 747.
With no air-breathing engines, it will be flown to a powerless landing, like a glider.
Houston is go for sep, have a great flight...
The tests demonstrated that the shuttle has acceptable landing performance.
during one of five free flights carried out at the Dryden Flight Research Facility, Edwards, Calif., in 1977.

description:
NASA's first shuttle orbiter, Enterprise, separates from the back of a Boeing 747 and glides to a landing on the dry lakebed at Edwards, California, during the 1977 approach and landing tests.
